Named for French botanist Jerome Triana and designated the national flower of Colombia, this classic large-flowered cattleya species produces broad, ruffled, fragrant lavender-pink petals surrounding a deep magenta-and-gold throat, blooming naturally in December in its high-elevation Colombian Andes habitat and giving the plant its common English name. A cooler-growing cattleya than many tropical lowland relatives, reflecting its native mountain cloud-forest habitat, it appreciates a distinct temperature drop at night and does not thrive in constant hot, humid lowland warmth. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, provide bright light with some direct morning sun for reliable flowering, and give the plant a cooler night temperature if possible to encourage its natural winter bloom cycle.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in fine, fast-draining orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Twinkle oncidium's small, mounted-friendly size and modest water needs make it well suited to a windowsill collection.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in fine, fast-draining orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Twinkle oncidium's small, mounted-friendly size and modest water needs make it well suited to a windowsill collection. This popular miniature hybrid produces sprays of numerous small, star-shaped white, pink, or yellow flowers with an intense, sweet vanilla-like fragrance that belies the plant's diminutive size, blooming reliably even on a young, small specimen unlike many larger orchid hybrids that take years to reach flowering maturity. Its compact size makes it one of the easiest oncidium-type orchids for a limited windowsill or grow-light collection, tolerating slightly less light than larger cattleya-alliance orchids while still flowering dependably multiple times a year. Water when the mix approaches dryness, feed lightly with a diluted orchid fertilizer during active growth, and repot every one to two years once the fine bark mix breaks down.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; spider orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11. Extraordinarily long, narrow, wavy-margined, pale green to yellow-green petals and sepals radiate outward from each flower in a dramatic, spidery silhouette that gives the species its common name, dotted with warty green markings near the flower's center that are believed to mimic spiders and attract wasp pollinators seeking prey. Native to Central American cloud forests, it thrives with the same intermediate warmth and bright, filtered light as many other epiphytic orchids, and its unusual, architectural flower form makes it a striking specimen even among a broader orchid collection. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, feed lightly with a balanced orchid fertilizer during active growth, and provide bright indirect light for the most reliable flowering.

planting.note: Grow as a shaded houseplant in a well-drained, moisture-retentive terrestrial orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Insigne slipper orchid is one of the more cold-tolerant paphiopedilum species and prefers cooler winter temperatures than tropical lowland orchids.

directions: Grow as a shaded houseplant in a well-drained, moisture-retentive terrestrial orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Insigne slipper orchid is one of the more cold-tolerant paphiopedilum species and prefers cooler winter temperatures than tropical lowland orchids. One of the original slipper orchid species that helped launch the popularity of the genus among Victorian-era orchid collectors, it produces a single striking flower per stem, with mottled coppery-green, twisted petals framing a large, glossy, pouch-shaped maroon-brown lip, the distinctive 'slipper' that gives the whole genus its common name. Native to cool, humid forests in the Himalayan foothills, it tolerates and even prefers cooler conditions than many tropical orchids, making it a good choice for a cooler room or unheated sunroom rather than a hot, humid greenhouse. Keep the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, provide bright indirect light rather than direct sun, and repot every one to two years as the terrestrial mix breaks down.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; violet moth orchid needs consistent warmth (65-85°F) and cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; violet moth orchid needs consistent warmth (65-85°F) and cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Thick, waxy, star-shaped flowers in rich violet-purple with a contrasting white or green center carry an intense, sweet fragrance most noticeable in the warmth of midday, opening just one or two at a time from a short stem rather than the long arching sprays typical of the hybrid moth orchids commonly sold in stores. Native to the hot, humid lowland rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, it requires warmer year-round temperatures than most commercial phalaenopsis hybrids, thriving best in a warm greenhouse or bright bathroom where heat and humidity stay consistently high. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity and warmth above 65°F even at night, and provide bright but filtered light for the best flowering and fragrance.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; Cooktown orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11. Australia's floral emblem for the state of Queensland, this warm-growing dendrobium species produces long, arching sprays of flat, moth-shaped flowers in shades of purple, pink, or white, closely resembling the more commercially familiar phalaenopsis orchids in flower shape, which inspired both its species name and common comparisons between the two genera. It has been extensively hybridized to create the widely available and easy-to-grow 'phalaenopsis-type' dendrobium hybrids commonly sold in garden centers, valued for their long-lasting sprays of flowers and relatively straightforward care compared to some more demanding orchid genera. Water more generously than cooler-growing dendrobiums, since this warm species does not need the pronounced dry winter rest that many other dendrobiums require, and provide bright, filtered light for the best bloom.

planting.note: Mount on bark or grow in a shallow, fast-draining orchid basket in bright, indirect to direct light; fringed star orchid needs strong light and good air movement to bloom, more sun than most cattleya-alliance relatives tolerate.

directions: Mount on bark or grow in a shallow, fast-draining orchid basket in bright, indirect to direct light; fringed star orchid needs strong light and good air movement to bloom, more sun than most cattleya-alliance relatives tolerate. Large, pale green to cream flowers are edged with an extraordinary, deeply fringed, lacy lip that looks almost hand-cut, opening with an intense, sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening that has made this species one of the most important parents used in breeding fragrant hybrid cattleyas. Native to Central American dry forests where it grows exposed to strong light on tree branches, it needs considerably more direct sun than most orchids to flower well, along with excellent drainage and air movement around its roots to prevent rot. Mount on a slab or grow in a basket with minimal, very fast-draining medium, water thoroughly then allow to dry quickly, and provide the strongest light the plant will tolerate without leaf burn for reliable flowering.

planting.note: Grow in a slatted basket with minimal or no potting medium in bright, indirect to direct light, watering daily in warm weather; Ascocenda needs consistent warmth, high humidity, and excellent air movement around its exposed roots.

directions: Grow in a slatted basket with minimal or no potting medium in bright, indirect to direct light, watering daily in warm weather; Ascocenda needs consistent warmth, high humidity, and excellent air movement around its exposed roots. A man-made hybrid genus combining Ascocentrum and Vanda, it produces compact plants with the same thick, exposed aerial roots as its Vanda parent, bearing flat, rounded, brilliantly colored flowers in shades of orange, pink, red, and purple, often patterned with a distinctive tessellated or checkered pattern, on a more compact, manageable scale than full-sized vanda hybrids. Popular in warm, humid tropical and subtropical gardens as well as greenhouse collections, it is typically grown bare-root or in an open slatted basket rather than a conventional pot, since its thick roots need constant air exposure and dry out quickly between frequent waterings. Water or mist daily in warm weather since the exposed roots have no reservoir of moist medium to draw from, feed weekly with a diluted orchid fertilizer, and provide strong light for the most vivid flower color.
